etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Scots glamour (“magic”), alteration of Middle English gramere (“grammar”), from Old French gramaire. Doublet of glamoury, gramarye, grammar, and grimoire. A connection has also been suggested with Old Norse glámr (“the moon", also "the name of a ghost”, poetic byname, literally “the pale one”) and glámsýni (“glamour, illusion”, literally “glam-sight”). From Grettir's Saga aka Grettis Saga, one of the Sagas of Icelanders, after the hero has been cursed by Glam, aka Glamr: "...he was become so fearsome a man in the dark, that he durst go nowhither alone after nightfall, for then he seemed to see all kinds of horrors. And that has fallen since into a proverb, that "Glam lends eyes", or gives Glamsight to those who see things nowise as they are."

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Originally, enchantment; magic charm; especially, the effect of a spell that causes one to see objects in a form that differs from reality, typically to make filthy, ugly, or repulsive things seem beauteous.

quote.citation: 1882, James Thomson (B. V.), The City of Dreadful Night:
quote.text: They often murmur to themselves, they speakTo one another seldom, for their woeBroods maddening inwardly and scorns to wreakItself abroad; and if at whiles it growTo frenzy which must rave, none heeds the clamour,Unless there waits some victim of like glamour,To rave in turn, who lends attentive show.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Alluring beauty or charm (often with sex appeal).
(uncountable) Any excitement, appeal, or attractiveness associated with a person, place, or thing; that which makes something appealing.

quote.citation: 1899 February, Joseph Conrad, “The Heart of Darkness”, in Blackwood’s Edinburgh Magazine, volume CLXV, number M, New York, N.Y.: The Leonard Scott Publishing Company, […], →OCLC, part I, page 197:
quote.text: “The North Pole was one of these places, I remember. Well, I haven’t been there yet, and shall not try now. The glamour’s off.”

quote.citation: 1950 May 7, The Daily Telegraph, Sydney, page 13, column 3:
quote.text: Boys have not lost their love for adventure, and still have `itchy feet.' Many are seeking glamor jobs, want to be writers, detectives, seamen.

definitions.definition: Any artificial interest in, or association with, objects, or persons, through which they appear delusively magnified or glorified.
A kind of haze in the air, causing things to appear different from what they really are.[1]

quote.citation: 1861 October, “The Nelumbium Luteum, or Yellow Egyptian Lotus.”, in Thomas Meehan, editor, The Gardner’s Monthly and Advertiser Horticultural, volume III, number 10, 23 North Sixth Street, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States, page 311:
quote.text: When the golden October comes, with its witching of hazy air that makes a glamour for all things and any landscape, we shall see these offspring of poetic myth stretch out beside the creeks, breaking the tender hulls for their magical chincapins, and feeding on them and on the dreams of which they are the talismans.

definitions.definition: (countable) An item, motif, person, image that by association improves appearance.
